extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, and researchers interested in presidential social media use and platform responses
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing presidential tweets and platform responses
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating tweets by a sitting president (authenticity, official status, factual accuracy, policy impact) and how platforms, institutions, and the public treat or respond to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tweets as official presidential statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a President's tweets count as official statements (e.g., 'Spicer: Tweets are Trump's official statements'; 'DOJ says Trump's tweets are official presidential statements').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the White House or DOJ treats a tweet as an official statement; consider press secretary/agency positions and legal/administrative interpretations cited on the page. The page documents debate and differing institutional views about tweet officialdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tweets as presidential records / archival requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether presidential tweets must be preserved as presidential records (e.g., 'Donald Trump's tweets are now presidential records').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a tweet is treated as an official record it triggers archiving and records-retention obligations; check references to archival actions and official statements about preserving tweets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform enforcement for civic-integrity/policy violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether particular tweets violate platform policies such as Twitter's Civic Integrity policy (e.g., Twitter required removal 'for repeated and severe violations of our Civic Integrity policy').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tweets against explicit platform policies (civic_integrity, election_misinformation, etc.); the page cites examples where Twitter removed tweets for policy violations and announced removals publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account suspension for risk of incitement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a platform may suspend or permanently ban an account citing 'risk of further incitement of violence' (e.g., 'Permanent suspension of @realDonaldTrump' citing risk of further incitement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider platform rationales and thresholds for severe enforcement (public safety/incitement). The page includes Twitter's public statement explaining suspension as prevention of further harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-check labels and disputed-content flags
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and when platforms add fact-check labels to false or disputed statements (e.g., 'Twitter Adds Fact-Check Labels To Trump's False Statements'; references to posts flagged as 'disputed' or misleading).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess factual accuracy and reliance on third-party fact-checkers; the page documents application of labels and tracking of how many posts were flagged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-interest exception to enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: When platforms apply a 'public-interest exception' to retain or not remove content from prominent public figures despite policy violations (e.g., 'About public-interest exceptions on Twitter').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a tweet is preserved under public-interest rationale; the page cites Twitter guidance about exceptions for public-interest content and related archival/visibility decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tweet authorship and account authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a tweet was posted by the account owner or someone else (e.g., 'How To Tell When Someone Else Tweets From @realDonaldTrump').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for metadata, timing, stylistic cues, and official explanations; the page references guides and reporting on identifying when tweets originate from the principal versus staff or other actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether tweets constitute formal orders or binding directives
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a tweet should be treated as a formal order (e.g., 'Secretary of Navy says Trump's tweet is not a formal order' contrasted with pieces noting tweets as official statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh institutional/legal statements from agencies and officials about whether a tweet has legal force; the page shows inconsistent positions across actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tweets as diplomacy/foreign-policy signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether tweets function as notifications or signals in foreign policy (e.g., North Korea and Iran threat tweets described as serving as notification or clarification of policy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the substance and timing of tweets for their diplomatic impact; the page cites media and government reactions to tweets aimed at foreign actors or crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retweets and amplification of extremist or fringe content
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether retweeting content elevates extremist or fringe actors (e.g., 'Donald Trump retweets Britain First deputy leader's Islamophobic posts' and commentary that retweets 'elevate' such groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat retweets as potential endorsements/amplification; assess provenance and extremist links. The page catalogs reactions and condemnations when the account amplified far-right content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tweets that encourage or allude to violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a tweet encourages, alludes to, or normalizes violence (e.g., tweets described as 'encourages violence against reporters' and videos of 'beating' media).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether content explicitly or implicitly incites harm; the page includes press and institutional condemnations and platform reactions to such tweets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tweets spreading misinformation or conspiracy theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether tweets spread demonstrably false claims or conspiracies (examples include Antifa conspiracy about injured Buffalo protester, false claims about elections, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check claims against fact-checking outlets referenced on the page; the page records numerous fact-checks and media analyses identifying false or misleading tweets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tweets that attempt to delegitimize democratic processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether tweets attempt to delegitimize elections or suggest improper changes to electoral processes (e.g., tweeting about delaying the election or claiming the Vice President can 'reject fraudulently chosen electors').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess constitutional and legal impossibilities and the political consequences; the page cites rebukes from politicians and legal commentary when tweets challenged electoral norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tweets' impact on public opinion and political standing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether tweets affect approval ratings, public perception, or political agenda (e.g., polls and commentary noting tweets 'hurting agenda' or lowering approval).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use polls, media analysis, and public response documented on the page to evaluate the political costs or benefits of particular tweets and patterns of tweeting.
